content_selection.rationale: Most of the included stories are solid and timely. The CERT-In multi-provider agent incident, the AI debt-financing squeeze, Rubin's AgentPerf results, Reflection's Beam and the disputed Replit/Anthropic split all hold up; I checked Replit and it was widely picked up, with the dispute properly noted. However, two important stories were dropped. One is Anthropic giving METR employee-level access to its systems, a major safety-governance development covered by Reuters, the FT and TechCrunch that has more lasting significance than the included Anthropic election-usage figures. The other is the FBI arrest of an OpenAI engineer over a bug planted in an executive conference room, which got broad national coverage and was excluded only because it was 'not verified in detail'. The brief also leans heavily on single preprints and vendor benchmarks (RealtimeBench, OpenGCUA, Glimpse) at the expense of these higher-impact policy and security stories.
content_selection.evidence: Excluded: "Anthropic independent evaluators update / METR employee-level access (Oct 15)" and "FBI arrests OpenAI employee over hidden recording device (headline only; not verified in detail)". Included instead: "Anthropic says 0.51% of sampled US Claude.ai conversations concern elections... (October 14)".

selection_disagreements.story: Anthropic grants METR employee-level access / independent evaluators update (Oct 15)
selection_disagreements.rationale: Reuters, the FT and TechCrunch all covered this. Anthropic gave six METR researchers company hardware, office space and internal-tool access comparable to its own risk teams. METR can also publish without Anthropic's approval, apart from narrow redactions, and it is the first top-tier evaluator under the White House Accord commitments. That makes it a significant safety-governance story, more consequential than the included election-usage stats, and nothing indicates it was covered in an earlier brief.

selection_disagreements.story: FBI arrests OpenAI engineer over hidden recording device in executive conference room
selection_disagreements.rationale: My searches found that Reuters, CBS, the Washington Post, Fortune and Fox all reported the DOJ charges on Oct 13. The suspect is a Saudi national charged with intercepting communications, and FBI Director Patel framed the case as a national-security matter involving 'super intelligence tech'. The story was easy to verify, contrary to the stated exclusion reason, and the candidate list doesn't mark it as covered in a prior brief. It warranted at least a short item or follow-up in the Policy/Security section.

selection_disagreements.story: Anthropic: preparing for the 2026 US midterms (election conversation stats, Oct 14)
selection_disagreements.rationale: This is a routine, self-reported usage statistic from Oct 14, so it's older and lower impact than the METR access announcement from the same company that was dropped. If space for an Anthropic policy item was limited, the METR story was the stronger pick.

factual_accuracy.rationale: I checked the brief against the primary sources it cites: the TechCrunch articles on India, Replit and Elorian, the Microsoft Research Magnetar blog, Artificial Analysis's Beam and Vera Rubin pages, the Apple MLX post, both Axios articles, Vercel's gateway index, the arXiv/GitHub pages for OpenGCUA and RealtimeBench, Anthropic's midterms post, and the PostgreSQL 19 coverage. Every number, date and attribution I checked matched, including the hedges: the brief says insiders dispute Replit's claim, marks Glimpse's wins as vendor-reported, and labels Magnetar, OpenGCUA and RealtimeBench as authors' unreplicated results. I found only small issues. Vercel's index says almost one in three 'teams' switched their most-used lab, and the brief adds the word 'paid'. Two Axios details (Meta receives no prompt data; the months-long collaboration) were only partly corroborated in the snippets I could see. Neither changes the substance.
factual_accuracy.evidence: "Artificial Analysis gives it 30 on its Intelligence Index, second among US open-weight models behind Meta's Muse Spark Open (39), and third outside China once the UAE's K2 Horizon (31) is counted; NVIDIA's Nemotron 3.5 Super VL scores 26." This matches the AA article exactly.

length_format.rationale: The brief has 14 Headlines bullets, inside the 8-15 range. It has 10 deep-dive items (Research 3, Industry 3, Products 1, Benchmarks 2, Policy 1), which sits at the top of the 5-10 range without exceeding it. Each deep-dive runs 5-6 sentences, within the 3-6 target, though several sentences are long and packed. All five tiered sections have content, so no empty-section issue arises, and the only minor skimmability drag is the long 'Follow-up' clauses on several headline bullets.
length_format.evidence: 14 headline bullets; deep-dives: Magnetar, Glimpse, OpenGCUA / Debt, Vera Rubin, Replit / Apple MLX / Beam, RealtimeBench / CERT-In = 10 items, each ~5-6 sentences ending in 'Why it matters:'

dedup.rationale: Every story in today's brief that touches prior coverage is explicitly flagged as a follow-up with the prior edition's date, and each adds substantive new reporting. The CERT-In India disclosure is a new incident with multiple providers. The debt item adds FT issuance figures ($23B vs $113B), Gartner forecasts and the Oracle loan stress. The Apple MLX item adds new throughput and memory measurements that correct the 10-16 framing. The remaining stories (Magnetar, Vera Rubin, Replit, Glimpse, OpenGCUA, RealtimeBench, PostgreSQL, Anthropic elections, Vercel) have no counterpart in the prior editions. The only recycled detail is CoreWeave's ~15% drop and Anthropic's Q3 cash-flow positivity from 10-15, which appear as context inside a labelled, substantively new follow-up.
